newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Chiroscience in U.S. asthma pill pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Chiroscience in U.S. asthma pill pact.

text.p: Britain's Chiroscience Group Plc said on Friday it agreed to work with U.S. firm Schering-Plough Corp to develop a new class of pills to treat asthma and other diseases.
Chiroscience said it stood to receive up to $38 million from the deal, mostly in the form of milestone payments, with about $2.0 million of that allotted for research and development.
The company will also receive royalties on product sales, while Schering would receive exclusive worldwide rights to all products from the collaboration.
"This agreement comes at an optimum time for our programme, just as planning for large-scale trials in asthma patients is beginning," said Chiroscience chief executive Dr. John Padfield.
The deal should also help boost Chiroscience's results this year, he told Reuters in an interview.
The drug discovery company's shares surged more than six percent on the news, rising 15 pence to 252.5 to rank among the top percentage gainers on the London Stock Exchange at 1055 GMT.
The agreement aimed to build on Chiroscience's preliminary success in treating asthma with a compound called D4418, part of a group known as PDE IV inhibitors.
These inhibitors, which target the phosphodiesterase type IV enzyme, suppress the body's reaction to foreign substances during asthma attacks.
"Asthma is an overreaction to a challenge, and what these compounds do is dampen down that overreaction," director of development Brian Gennery told Reuters.
Unlike conventional asthma medicines, the inhibitors would be administered as a pill rather than inhaled through aerosol inhalers.
The company expected to report results from its Phase I trial of D4418 in October.

That trial, involving about 20 patients in northern England, will show whether Chiroscience's compound can be used without causing nausea and vomiting -- the side effects that have hampered other firms' research.

"What we're aiming to demonstrate in Phase I is that there's no nausea and vomiting, or if it occurs, it occurs at a very, very high dose where it wouldn't be a problem commercially," Padfield said, adding that animal studies had indicated minimal side effects.
If successful, the company would start Phase II trials on D4418 in 1998/99, with an asthma product possibly reaching the market in the early part of the next decade.
Under the Schering-Plough deal, the companies also planned to develop PD IV inhibitors to treat ailments such as chronic bronchitis and rheumatoid arthritis.
For its part, Chiroscience expected significantly better results this year, boosted by the U.S. pact and its profitable technical services operation, ChiroTech.
"Clearly the earnings this year will be significantly more than they were last year," Padfield said.
Chiroscience posted an operating loss of 21.0 million pounds ($35 million) for the year ended February 28 compared to a loss of 13.1 million pounds the previous year.
Padfield said the firm had about 50 million pounds of cash, which it expected to spend at a rate of some 25 million pounds a year.
"For this coming year our burn rate of roughly two million pounds (net) a month should be roughly the same as last year," he said.
"We have sufficient cash to meet our current business requirements. We have no current intention to return to the equity market for more cash," he added. ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
